title: She did not say it. There is no evidence Marie Antoinette ever said let them eat cake.
description:
There is no evidence Marie Antoinette ever said let them eat cake. Historians treat the line as a cliché that was attached to her later.

Wrote the line in his Confessions about an unnamed great princess, and may have invented the anecdote. It was published in 1782.

When Rousseau wrote it, Marie Antoinette was nine years old. She had not yet left Austria. She did not arrive in France until 1770.

The French word is brioche, a luxury bread enriched with butter and eggs. Cake is the traditional English translation.

A French writer who attributed the line to Marie Antoinette in print, about fifty years after her death.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let_them_eat_cake (read): established that the line first appears in Rousseau's Confessions, whose first six books were written in 1765 and published in 1782; that Rousseau attributed it to an unnamed great princess and may have invented the anecdote; that Marie Antoinette was nine in 1765 and had not yet come from Austria; that Alphonse Karr attributed it to her in Les Guêpes in 1843; that the words are about brioche, an enriched bread; that other people were blamed earlier, including a 7th century Chinese emperor in the Book of Jin; and that historians find no evidence she said it.
- https://www.history.com/news/did-marie-antoinette-really-say-let-them-eat-cake (read): corroborated that the story circulated before 1789, was first told about Marie Therese, a Spanish princess who married Louis XIV, that Rousseau included it in the Confessions, and that historians say Marie Antoinette did not say it. It gives the details of the wording and year of Rousseau slightly differently from Wikipedia, so those details are not used.
